query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature conditions is governed by their high configurational entropy—which raises atomic diffusion barriers—and by the formation of strong, defect-mediated interfacial bonds with engineered supports, which together inhibit sintering and chemical segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles prepared via standard chemical routes with uniform distribution of constituent elements and low noble-metal content.
generation.intervention: Conduct in situ high-temperature TEM experiments comparing nanoparticles supported on defect-engineered substrates (designed to provide numerous high-energy bonding sites) with those on inert supports. Simultaneously perform atomistic simulations to predict diffusion barriers and binding energies at the nanoparticle–support interface.
generation.conditions: Evaluate performance in controlled atmospheres over the temperature ranges relevant for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectrics (473–1923 K), while keeping nanoparticle composition and noble-metal content constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The defect-rich engineered support that provides robust anchoring points for the nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: The intrinsic chemical disorder (high configurational entropy) in the nanoparticles elevates the energy barrier for atomic diffusion and sintering, while the defect sites on the engineered support interact strongly with the nanoparticle surfaces, further stabilizing their structure and chemistry at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles on defect-engineered supports will exhibit significantly reduced sintering, aggregation, and compositional segregation compared to those on inert supports under identical high-temperature treatments.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles deposited on inert supports without engineered defect sites will show a higher rate of particle coalescence and chemical inhomogeneity due to unmitigated surface diffusion at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This stabilization effect is expected only when the density of support defects is sufficient to overcome the thermal energy in the specified temperature ranges and may not apply if the alloy composition deviates markedly from near-equiatomic ratios or under reactive (e.g., oxidizing) environments.
generation.uncertainty: While the direction of the effect is predicted based on energetics and support interactions, the precise magnitudes of diffusion barrier enhancement and stabilization benefits remain uncertain due to variations in support material properties and nanoparticle microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two identical sets of nanoparticles and deposit them separately on defect-engineered supports and inert supports. Expose both samples to identical high-temperature treatments within the specified ranges while conducting in situ TEM imaging and complementary atomistic simulations. Compare the evolution of particle size, morphology, and chemical composition over time.
measurements: TEM imaging to quantify nanoparticle size and aggregation state
EDS mapping for assessing compositional homogeneity
Simulated diffusion barrier estimates at the nanoparticle-support interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles on both engineered and inert supports display similar extents of sintering, aggregation, or chemical inhomogeneity after high-temperature treatment within the experimental error, then the hypothesis that defect-mediated support interactions confer enhanced stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. Since the successful fabrication of the first-ever entropy- stabilized oxides, or, more general, high-entropy oxides (HEOs), such solid solutions have drawn much attention due to their unique compositional and structural features, namely, the extreme chemical disorder incorporated into single-crystal structures (). One representative example is that the metal ions in (Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)O are unanimously divalent and randomly occupy the cationic sites in a rocksalt structure. These cations are coordinated by lattice oxygen in an octahedral configuration, even though Cu(II) and Zn(II) are usually four coordinated to oxygen atoms as, for example, in their binary oxides (). This stabilization of Cu(II) and Zn(II) in an unfavorable configuration is ascribable to the increased configurational entropy and a high solid solution temperature (, , ). Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions.
